sections.h2: Why selling in Port St. Lucie is different
sections.html:
Port St. Lucie is a very large, very young city in St. Lucie County, with a July 2025 population estimate of 268,062, up 30.9 percent from the April 2020 base. The city expects another 125,000 residents over the next 10 to 15 years.

All that growth puts new construction near almost every street, and your house competes with it. Buyers can line yours up against a fresh build, so condition and price both count. Most sellers choose one of three routes.

Before choosing, list what you know about the house: roof and air conditioner age, any septic system, open permits, HOA dues and who lives there. A cash buyer discounts for problems, and a retail buyer finds them in an inspection, so being upfront saves time either way.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure to buyers, along with repair requests.
  • Owner-handled sale: lower cost, with the paperwork on you.
  • Cash offer: a fit for deferred work, a vacancy or a short timeline.

Port St. Lucie was incorporated in 1961 by a development group whose goal was selling quarter-acre lots to retirees, without sidewalks, streetlights, water or sewer. General Development Corporation turned 66 square miles into mostly single-family lots in the 1960s, and later growth reached St. Lucie West and land west of I-95.

That layout explains why many early lots were sold without sewer service. The city runs one of the country's larger septic-to-sewer conversion projects, so ask the city utility about the sewer status of your street. A buyer will ask, and a cash buyer will price in any septic work.

sections.h2: Property taxes and Save Our Homes
sections.html:
Only 22 percent of a typical bill goes to the city. The county, school district, fire district and other bodies take the rest. The St. Lucie County Property Appraiser reassesses each January 1, and a buyer does not inherit the prior owner's exemptions and caps, which can push the bill up.

Under Save Our Homes, a homestead's yearly increase stops at 3 percent or CPI, whichever is smaller, and the savings start building after the first homestead year. Applications and renewals are accepted from January 1 through March 1. A homestead cannot be moved to a new residence.

Voters passed Amendment 3 on November 3, 2026, which enlarges the non-school homestead exemption from 2027. The St. Lucie office can tell you how it applies to your parcel.

  • Bills go out in early November, with discounts of 4 percent in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February.
  • Unpaid taxes become delinquent on April 1.
  • Have the title agent prorate this year's bill at closing.

When a lender forecloses through the courts, the clerk auctions the property 20 to 35 days after final judgment, unless the plaintiff agrees to wait longer (section 45.031). The top bidder leaves a 5 percent deposit, and if no objection comes within 10 days of the certificate of sale, the clerk files the certificate of title.

A homestead owner should ask the clerk about surplus funds within 10 days after the sale. Closing a private sale before the auction may leave more equity with you, so call a lender or attorney the moment a judgment issues. After a foreclosure, the certificate of title is taxed on the highest bid.

Outside Miami-Dade, Florida taxes a deed at 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and a mortgage the buyer takes on counts as part of it. All parties are liable, so the contract should decide who pays. The clerk collects the tax at recording.

Section 689.01 requires two subscribing witnesses for a land conveyance, and audio-video technology can be used to witness the signing.

  • Get a payoff letter from each lender.
  • Check city records for open permits on sheds, pools, enclosures or additions.
  • Gather HOA or special-district statements if the neighborhood has them.

Heat and humidity make air-conditioning age and roof condition major points in a buyer's inspection. Homes near the North Fork of the St. Lucie River or canals raise insurance and flood-zone questions, so keep your policy and any permit records for roof, window and enclosure work on hand.

If your house is a short drive from the river, mention trail and park access in your description. Buyers compare those amenities with newer neighborhoods farther west.

1. Give the buyer the address, payoff amount and any tenant or vacancy details.
  2. Read each written offer for price, repair terms and closing day.
  3. The title agent searches the record and asks lenders for payoffs.
  4. Sign the deed with two witnesses present.
  5. The clerk records it, and you get your money.

With no buyer's lender involved, title drives the timeline. Plan on a few days for payoffs, HOA statements and the signing.

faqs.q: Is a cash offer realistic for a Port St. Lucie house?
faqs.a: Yes, especially for a house that needs work or has a deadline. Cash buyers skip lender appraisals, but title must be clear and the deed witnessed and recorded.

faqs.q: Does a buyer inherit my homestead exemption in Port St. Lucie?
faqs.a: No. The buyer's assessment drops your exemptions and caps, and homestead does not carry over to a new residence.

faqs.q: How long until a foreclosure sale after judgment?
faqs.a: Usually 20 to 35 days under section 45.031, unless the plaintiff agrees to longer. A sale that closes first can protect your equity.

faqs.q: Who pays documentary stamps on the deed?
faqs.a: Your contract decides, though state rules make every party liable. Outside Miami-Dade the rate is 70 cents per $100.

faqs.q: What share of my tax bill is the city's?
faqs.a: The city's share is about 22 percent. The county, school district, fire district and other taxing bodies get the rest.
